text.p: A Dutch father and son, a Thai special Olympian born without legs and a former British soldier crippled by a mine blast took major honours at the first Phnom Penh International Marathon on Sunday.

Cambodian runners were not disgraced in the biggest marathon in this southeast Asian nation since peace was signed in 1991, taking three of the top five places in a race run under a strong sun on a flat course leading into the capital.

Neals Strik, 23, who had decided only the night before to run his first full marathon, took first place with a respectable time of two hours, 40 minutes and six seconds while his father Rob came in fifth at 3:06:15 to win the men's veteran (over 40s) trophy.

Cambodia's leading distance runner came in second with a time of 2:41:16, followed by compatriots Huot Peou and Chheng Piseth in a race that counted as the national marathon championship for all locals taking part.
Strik pulled ahead of To Rithya at the 25 km (15 mile) mark and managed to keep the lead despite the heat.
The race was completed by 30 individual runners, a team of people who had been injured by mines and 10 wheelchair racers.
"I thought I would be a winner in the first 20 kms, but I didn't have enough power...I became weaker," To Rithya said.
The day's most impressive performance came from world-class wheelchair racer Prasopchoke Klunngern of Thailand.
The Thai, who was born without legs, beat the whole field home in just 1:42:12 in his U.S.-made racing chair. Nine Cambodians finished in the wheelchair event.

"The road was not so good in some places...I drank a lot of water because it was very hot," said the Thai, who came in fifth in the marathon and won a 10,000 metres bronze medal at the Atlanta Paralympics last year.

Briton Chris Moon came in last with a time of around six hours and 20 minutes, an hour slower than his record in last year's New York marathon but a stirring performance less than two years after losing his right leg and forearm to a mine blast in Mozambique.
He was paced by a relay team of Cambodian mine clearing specialists, all amputees, who each raced one kilometre.
"It's the flu that killed me and I just had no energy," said Moon, who used to work in Cambodia as a mine clearance expert for Britain's Halo Trust. He vowed to be back in 1997.
Sunday's event included races of 3km, 10km and a half marathon for able-bodied and handicapped competitors, including amputees.
Cambodia is among the most heavily-mined countries in the world.
